chapter_theme: In the Mokkala debate Neelakesi and the Buddhist elder Mokkalan argue whether the soul that gives and does penance is the one rewarded in heaven, whether a thing can change yet persist, whether a quality leaves its substance (the flower's scent in a pot), what release is and why the freed do not return, and whether the Jina can know all things in all times at once and speak without karma.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddhist elder at Padumapuram, called the thera (தேரன்)

415.reading: Neelakesi argues that if the soul stays joined with the body it has taken, seeing and knowing are rightly said to belong to the soul that is there, and calls Mokkalan unlearned: for him, who has only the heap of the body, the working of that heap goes wrong.
415.nuance: பிண்டம் (the lump or heap) is her word for what the Buddhist puts in place of a soul; the point is that perception needs a perceiver dwelling in the body, not a mere aggregate.

claims.claim: seeing and knowing belong to the soul that abides joined with the body

416.reading: Mokkalan replies that she holds the soul to be not other than the body in place, and objects that then no one can say today that the man who did great dharma, beginning with alms, becomes a god in the course he goes to, so all such deeds would be despised.
416.nuance: The objection takes the Jain teaching that the soul fills the body it occupies and argues that a soul bound to this body's place cannot be the one rewarded in heaven; 417 answers it.

claims.claim: a soul not other than the body in place cannot be the one that reaches heaven for its alms, so meritorious deeds lose their point

417.reading: Neelakesi answers that the same abiding soul is there when it goes about giving without stint, when it leaves pride and suffers to keep its vows, and when it is in heaven, and tells him to take this as the truth of giving.
417.nuance: She grounds the worth of giving (தானம்) on the identity of the giver across lives: the giver and the one in heaven are one soul. The value of the gift is made to rest on the reward reaching its doer.

claims.claim: the soul that gives and keeps vows is the same soul that later dwells in heaven, which is what makes giving true

418.reading: Mokkalan says she shows that a thing has no being at a time other than its own, and argues, addressing her as the woman with scented tresses, that then the good soul of a world-famed ascetic would not exist in the time to come, and keeping the precepts would be wasted toil.
418.nuance: The first line can be construed in more than one way; read here as his statement of her view that each state of a thing exists in its own time, turned against continuity of reward.

claims.claim: if a thing exists only in its own time, the ascetic's soul will not exist in the future and keeping precepts is vain

419.reading: Neelakesi answers that whether the soul is suffering in austerity, guarding hard vows, fasting and wasting away, or is called an exalted unblinking god, its being stays with it in each of its times.
419.nuance: இமையான், the one who does not blink, is a god; the verse places the ascetic and the god he becomes on one line of a single soul's existence.

claims.claim: the soul's existence abides through each of its states, from austerity to divine birth

420.reading: Mokkalan charges that she says one thing does not become another, and in the same breath teaches that milk becomes curd, so her words are like those of people who contradict themselves; the thera says those who do not understand think they are clear.
420.nuance: The first half-line (நூறான் இரும்பாய் நிகழாமை) seems to give her example of what does not become something else; its exact sense is not clear. The charge is against the Jain view that a thing both persists and changes.

claims.claim: to hold that a thing does not become another and yet that milk becomes curd is self-contradiction

421.reading: Neelakesi replies that she said suitable things become their effects by meeting their own causes, and asks whether she, like a madman, would say anything becomes anything; she tells him to speak along the line of the seed, and calls him a white elephant.
421.nuance: The seed (வித்து) is the model of change by proper cause. வெள் யானை may be a jibe at the white elephant of the Buddha's birth story, or simply an insult for a dull one; the text does not settle it.

claims.claim: a thing becomes its effect only through its own proper causes, not anything from anything

422.reading: Mokkalan says she holds that a quality cannot exist in a thing other than its own, and counters that the world says the scent which is the quality of the patala flower has passed into the potsherd; she spoke without examining, so let her claim go.
422.nuance: He appeals to common usage (வையம் உரைக்கின்றது) as evidence that a quality can move from its substance into another.

claims.claim: a quality can pass from its own substance into another, as a flower's scent into a pot

423.reading: The narrator tells how the peerless woman ended her answer by giving reasons to the Tathagata's man: even when a flower's scent sits in a new sherd, the wise say the fine scent is the flower's, for the flower's particles stay there and carry it.
423.nuance: தாதுக்கள் here are read as the flower's fine particles: the scent never leaves its substance, since bits of the flower lodge in the pot. ததாகதற்கு names the opponent by his master.
423.event: Neelakesi closes her reply on the flower's scent with reasons.

claims.claim: a scent in a pot remains the flower's, carried by particles of the flower

424.reading: Mokkalan takes up the place of release she desires, and asks, if she calls it good, what went there in the way the burning hell and the bright heaven, which they named together, are places one goes to.
424.nuance: The second line (நாயிற்கு) is obscure. The gist seems to be that a release located in a place is only one more destination like hell and heaven.

claims.claim: a release that is a place would be one more destination like hell and heaven

425.reading: Neelakesi retorts that his teacher spoke of six kinds of destinies and of heaps of aggregates as if they were places, and he shows them; if one says the place of release of those who have destroyed karma's fruit by rule is such, and he asks what it is, is the answer not scripture?
425.nuance: The verse has no closing என்றாள், so the speaker is inferred from the alternation. ஆகமம் here is the Jain scripture, not the Saiva Agamas. பாக்கனாய் is an obscure term of address.

claims.claim: the place of the released is known from scripture, as the Buddha himself named six destinies

426.reading: Mokkalan asks whether, if release is a birth-place from which none come back, the not-coming-back belongs to the place reached; and if she explains it by the absence of karma, he argues that if the freed one is the same who was bound, karma will reach him again.

claims.claim: if the released soul is the same one that was bound, karma can bind it again, so release by a lasting soul is not final

427.reading: Neelakesi says she does not call release a birth, nor say the place itself prevents return, nor that karmas cling merely because they exist; she holds that it is the unforgetting yoga activity that brings back the stain, and his words do not reach her.
427.nuance: யோக பாவம் is the Jain sense of yoga: the activity of body, speech and mind through which karma flows in. With that activity gone, nothing draws karma to the freed soul. Not the Saiva or Siddhar yoga of union.

claims.claim: karmic stain returns only through the activity (yoga) of body, speech and mind; the freed soul without it is not bound again

428.reading: Mokkalan argues that she calls this the excellent release while the soul still has knowledge that arises, continued being, and a clinging thought that takes outer objects; by such a soul there is no way to give up evil karma, good woman, and he challenges her to answer.

claims.claim: a released soul that still knows, persists and takes outer objects keeps the grounds of evil karma

429.reading: Neelakesi rejects every one of his unprofitable reasons, arguing that harm comes only where the binding activity stands, and that he understands nothing; let his speech end.
429.nuance: Lines 2 and 3 are obscure (யோடுகொடு, குன்றினில் கூர்ங்கை நாட்டால்); the reading takes them as an image of something that cannot harm where there is nothing to take hold, in line with 427.

claims.claim: knowing objects does not bind karma unless the binding activity is present

430.reading: Mokkalan says she holds that her Lord knows all endless things by knowledge without any instrument, and objects that endless knowledge itself is an inner instrument; he asks her, nectar to those who join her, to answer.
430.nuance: The Jain claim of omniscience without sense organs is stated here by the opponent; the objection is his.

claims.claim: the Jina's endless knowledge is itself an inner instrument, so his knowing is not free of instruments

431.reading: Neelakesi tells him to fix his mind on this: what are called instruments are karma and the partial knowledges that karma produces; impurity covers all but the Lord, and to think otherwise is like a crow trying to see the end of the roaring sea.
431.nuance: விகல ஞானங்கள் are the defective, sense-bound knowings that karma gives; the Lord's knowledge is not of that kind. The crow and the sea mock a limited knower claiming the whole.

claims.claim: instruments of knowing are karma and the partial knowledges karma produces; the Lord's complete knowledge needs none

432.reading: Mokkalan sets a dilemma: if the Lord has no organ, he has no speech either and is only like a mountain echo to those who throng and ask; if he has an organ and comes to those who ask, she will be calling good karma done long ago the Lord.

claims.claim: an omniscient Lord without organs cannot speak, and one with organs is only the fruit of past good karma

433.reading: Neelakesi answers that by the instrument called the body the Lord knows and tells what those who come to him ask, and asks whether karma can do that; then, though he may be angry, she tells the thera to go into the fire and wishes never to see his like even in a dream.
433.nuance: The curse in lines 3 and 4 marks the debate's heat; it is not an event, only speech.

claims.claim: the Lord speaks and answers through a body, which karma by itself cannot do

434.reading: Mokkalan argues that if the Lord knows not in order but all at once, then old age, youth and death, which never dwell together in one man, would be together in his knowledge, and his knowledge would rise upon what does not exist; let it be so then, swan-like one.
434.nuance: The objection is that knowing past and future at once means knowing what is not now real. The word division of line 4 (அன்ன மன்னாய்) is taken as அன்னம் அன்னாய்.

claims.claim: knowledge of all times at once would be knowledge of what does not exist

435.reading: Neelakesi answers that we see those of virtuous conduct who have won firm divine bodies show forth the three times, and he will not grasp that the Lord, wiser than the three worlds, knows them all the more; he has covered his mind.
435.nuance: The argument is a fortiori: if gods who reached heaven by virtue can show the three times, the Lord greater than they can.

claims.claim: if virtuous gods can show the three times, the Lord wiser than the three worlds knows them

436.reading: Mokkalan argues that a knowledge grasping at once all good things of all days in all their aspects would be like a good man with a good sword cutting all the stalks of the wet water creeper at one stroke; only if that can be would her word hold.
436.nuance: The image seems to be the cutting of many stalks that looks like one act but is a succession of cuts; the lines are hard to construe.

claims.claim: no knowing grasps all things in one act; what looks simultaneous is successive

437.reading: Neelakesi asks who ever learned from anyone that the moon is different in each pool of water or the sun has a different light in each town, and says the wise called the Lord such; what the thera said does not hold.
437.nuance: The moon one in all waters and the sun one over all towns answer 436: one undivided knowing is present to all things at once. அன்னம் in line 4 is hard to construe.

claims.claim: the Lord's knowing is one and present to all things at once, as one moon is in every water

438.reading: Mokkalan asks: if the Lord's knowledge grasps the countless things at once through a common quality present in all, then all their differences would be lost; and if their natures are not alike, how could knowledge take them all?
438.nuance: Neelakesi's reply comes in 439, the first verse of the next run, where she answers that things are grasped by being both alike and unlike.

claims.claim: a single grasp of all things either erases their differences through a common quality or cannot hold unlike things together

links.note: The Kural says giving alone is good even if there were no higher world; in 416-417 both debaters take the giver's reaching heaven as what makes giving worth doing, and Neelakesi calls the identity of giver and god the truth of giving (தானத்தின் உண்மை).
links.teaches: The Kural's 'even if there were no higher world' is a position neither the Jain nor the Buddhist debater will hold here, since both stake the worth of alms on a rewarded doer.

gains.a: The epic's grounding of giving in reward is shown to be a choice that another ethics declined.
gains.b: The couplet's hypothetical is seen against a real debate in which a giver without a future was taken to make giving void.

links.note: The Kural likens the body-life bond to a bird leaving its nest; Neelakesi holds the soul joined with the body it has taken and makes it the one who sees and knows there.
links.teaches: The Kural's bird stresses how loosely the life sits in the body, while the Jain debater insists the soul fills and works the body as its knower, so the same separability is put to opposite uses.

gains.a: The verse's soul is set against a familiar image of a life that merely lodges in the body and leaves.
gains.b: The bird-and-nest image is shown to leave open what does the knowing while the bird is in the nest, which the debate answers.

links.note: Against Kundalakesi (201) Neelakesi used the thread running through a garland for what carries knowledge from moment to moment; against Mokkalan (419) she says the soul's being stays through austerity, vows and divine birth.
links.teaches: The continuity argued against Kundalakesi for memory within one life is here stretched across births, because the reward of penance needs the same soul to arrive in heaven.

links.note: The Manimekalai's Jain debater says each thing is both lasting and passing and takes on origination, persistence and destruction in every moment; in 420-421 Mokkalan calls this self-contradiction (milk becomes curd), and Neelakesi answers that change runs only by a thing's own causes.
links.teaches: The Buddhist epic sets out the Jain both-lasting-and-passing doctrine unanswered, while the Jain epic shows the Buddhist charge against it and the reply, so together they show the doctrine and where it was attacked.

links.note: In 202 Neelakesi grants that the pathiri scent stays in the new pot after the flower decays, to argue a soul outlasting the body; in 422-423 Mokkalan cites the scent in the sherd as a quality leaving its substance, and she answers that the flower's particles stay and carry it.
links.teaches: The same pot-and-scent example cuts both ways in the Jain debater's hands: against Kundalakesi it shows something that endures, against Mokkalan she must deny that the scent ever left its substance.

links.note: Neelakesi says the Buddha himself spoke of six kinds of destinies; in the Manimekalai Aravanar teaches that beings are of six kinds (humans, gods, Brahmas, hell-beings, animals, ghosts), born by good and bad deeds.
links.teaches: Neelakesi's retort works because Buddhists did teach six realms on their master's word, as the Buddhist epic confirms, so her appeal to scripture for the place of release matches their own practice.

links.note: The Kural says those who have learned and seen the true thing reach the path of not coming back here; Mokkalan asks what makes non-return final, and Neelakesi answers that karma returns only through yoga activity, which the freed soul lacks.
links.teaches: The Kural names the path of no return without saying what keeps it closed, and the debate supplies a mechanism: return needs the inflow of karma through activity, which release has ended.

gains.a: The Jain answer is set against the general Tamil promise of a path of no return, showing which part of that promise it explains.
gains.b: The couplet's 'not coming back' is tested by the objection that a lasting freed self could be bound again.

links.note: The Manimekalai's Jain debater says release is blocking the way good and bad deeds come in and wearing out past deeds; Neelakesi names that way as yoga activity and uses it to deny that a freed soul could be rebound.
links.teaches: The inflow that the Buddhist epic's summary only mentions becomes, in the Jain epic, the answer to the charge that a released soul could fall back into bondage.

links.note: The narrator in 48 says the sage Munichandra knew without limit the things of the three times; in 435 Neelakesi argues that if virtuous gods can show the three times, the Lord must know them.
links.teaches: Her a-fortiori argument for the Lord's knowledge of the three times rests on lesser knowers the epic had already shown, including the human sage who converted her.

links.note: Tirumular says the undiscerning take the moon in clouds and in a pot of Ganga water as many, though it is one; Neelakesi asks who ever said the moon differs in each water, to show the Lord's one knowing present to all things.
links.teaches: Both use one moon in many waters, but the Saiva verse makes the many appearances one reality, while the Jain keeps the many things real and makes only the knowing single.

gains.a: The Jain image is seen to stop short of the oneness the same figure carries in Saiva teaching.
gains.b: Tirumular's moon is shown to be a shared figure the Jains used for knowledge, not only for the one Lord in many bodies.

new_concepts.gloss: formal debate between schools, opened by a challenge and held before a king's assembly
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam's rubric (மொக்கல வாதச் சருக்கம்); the id differs from vaadham, which the list already uses for alchemy

new_concepts.gloss: the gods as a class of embodied beings in the round of births, ranked and numbered beside humans, animals and hell-beings
a state or course of birth: in Jain teaching one of the four (hell, animal, human, god) into which deeds carry a soul
new_concepts.label_source: the verses' own words: செல் கதி (416), கதியின வகைய ஆறும் (425)

new_concepts.gloss: the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness) that are spoken of as a person
the Buddha: the awakened teacher of dharma, his coming in a dark age, and the worship of his seat and footprints
new_concepts.label_source: ததாகதற்கு (423); in 425 the Buddha is the one who spoke (சொன்னான்)

new_concepts.gloss: the vow; a religious observance or discipline undertaken

source_issues: 417 lines 3-4: the speech-close என்றா/டானத்தின் runs across the line break (என்றாள் தானத்தின்?), and the verse ends with a second என்றாள்.
424 line 2: நாயிற்கு is obscure; probably a corruption.
425: no closing என்றாள்/என்றான்; speaker inferred from the alternation; பாக்கனாய் obscure.
429 lines 2-3: யோடுகொடு and கூர்ங்கை are obscure, perhaps for யோகொடு.
431 line 4: என்லை is probably a misprint for எல்லை.
436 lines 2-4 and 437 line 4 (அன்னம்) are hard to construe.
